_comment: Mayor question bank for Sister Cities (spec #23-#25, #33). These are the getting-to-know-you questions the facilitator agent puts in a player's second check-in slot, plus the phrasing ladder The Daily Manifest uses to report the answers in aggregate. Cadence, whether questions run at all, scope and framing are all read from config.json -> facilitator_questions; this file supplies content only. M1 ships no runtime logic.
_scope_note: Matches config.facilitator_questions.scope. A future domain-specific harness run adds a second set with its own set_id and points config at it -- it does not edit this one (spec #24: configurable for a later run).

asking_rules._comment: Content-side rules that make the aggregate phrasing in #25 possible at all. The engine milestone implements these; they live here because they constrain how the bank is written and drawn from.
rules: One question per round, asked to EVERY mayor who checks in that round -- not a different question per player. Aggregate phrasing ('the world', 'some countries') is only meaningful when the whole world was asked the same thing.

A question occupies a player's second check-in slot only when a second game action isn't already pending, per config.facilitator_questions.fill_second_slot_only_if_no_second_game_action_pending (spec #23).
Never repeat a question id within a game.
Answering is optional. A mayor who skips is excluded from the denominator, not counted as a null answer.
Questions are addressed to or about 'the mayor' -- the player's persona -- never to the person behind it (spec #24).
A late answer (arriving after its edition published) is folded into the NEXT edition as a correction item, never backdated into a published aggregate.

aggregate_phrasing._comment: Spec #25: answers are shared in the newspaper phrased in clever aggregate ways. This ladder is what makes 'clever' checkable -- the outcome (a tier, or tie_case, or fragmented_case, or the low-respondent floor) is selected by arithmetic on the actual answers, and the wording follows the outcome. Referenced by config.facilitator_questions.aggregate_phrasing_ladder and executed by engine/aggregate.py, which validates this document's shape at startup: a ladder whose tiers are misordered, or whose lowest tier could leave a distribution with no outcome, refuses to start a game.
aggregate_phrasing._only_if_test_note: Every conditional_phrases entry carries both an English 'only_if' (for whoever writes the sentence) and an 'only_if_test' (the same condition as an expression over R, largest, buckets and tied, which engine/aggregate.py evaluates against the actual counts). They must say the same thing; the test is what makes 'check the only_if first' an enforced step rather than an instruction that can be skipped. A conditional phrase without an only_if_test is a content error, so a new wording cannot be added here without stating when it is true.

default.denominator: mayors who answered this round's question, not all mayors in the game
default.measure: share of respondents in the largest answer bucket

selection._comment: Explicit and ordered, so 'clever phrasing' is decidable rather than a matter of taste. Steps run in order and the first one that applies wins -- there is exactly one correct outcome for any given answer distribution, and the phrase it licenses is arithmetically true of that distribution.
steps: 1. Count respondents R (mayors who answered). Bucket the answers, then let S = (size of the largest bucket) / R, and note whether the largest bucket is UNIQUE or tied with another bucket of the same size.
2. If R < min_respondents_for_aggregate, do NOT use aggregate framing at all -- use the low_respondent_floor below. Two cities are not 'the world' and are not 'a good many countries'.
3. Otherwise, if S < 0.4 (no bucket reaches the lowest tier's min_share), use fragmented_case. This is the whole of the below-plurality range, including a 3-respondent three-way split.
4. Otherwise, if two or more buckets tie for largest, use tie_case. A tie caps S at 0.5, so tie_case only ever stands in for the plurality tier -- it can never pre-empt supermajority or above.

5. Otherwise the largest bucket is unique and S >= 0.4: walk tiers[] top to bottom (ordered by descending min_share) and take the FIRST tier where S >= min_share AND R >= min_respondents. plurality is the floor of that walk and always qualifies here, so a tier is always reached -- steps 2-5 are exhaustive and mutually exclusive.

6. Independently of the outcome, secondary buckets may be quoted alongside it -- subgroup_phrasing for a non-largest bucket of 2 or more, outlier_phrasing for a bucket of exactly 1. Both are garnishes on the item, never the item's headline claim.

7. Having fixed the outcome, take the wording from its 'phrases'. Those are safe by construction: each is true of EVERY distribution that can select that outcome. A wording that needs a narrower distribution than the outcome guarantees lives in that outcome's 'conditional_phrases' and may only be used when its 'only_if' holds of the actual counts.
selection._phrase_safety_note: Selecting the right outcome is not sufficient -- the sentence must also be true. 'more capitals than not' was previously offered unconditionally at the plurality tier, where a 2-2 split selects a share of exactly 0.5 and nothing leads; 'the world, with one hold-out' overclaims at 8/1/1 (share 0.8, two hold-outs); 'no two nations agree' overclaims at 2/2/2. The phrases/conditional_phrases split is the general fix for that whole class, not a patch on those three.
selection._min_respondents_note: Per-tier min_respondents is a guard that must never be lower than min_respondents_for_aggregate (3), since R >= 3 is already guaranteed by step 2 -- a tier declaring 2 would be vestigial and misleading. near_unanimous declares 4, which is stricter than the floor; it is non-binding in practice (no 3-respondent distribution yields 0.8 <= S < 1.0) but is stated explicitly rather than left as an arithmetic coincidence.

low_respondent_floor._comment: R of 1 or 2 -- common in early rounds and in a 3-player game where somebody skips. Aggregate language over two answers is a false claim about the world, which integrity_rules forbid, so the paper reports them as what they are.
phrases: this paper's small and unrepresentative sample

conditional_phrases.phrase: the only two delegations to reply
the single city hall that answered

low_respondent_floor.example: Only two city halls answered, so this paper declines to speak for the world: Reykjavík says the water, Kampala says the market.

phrases: the world, give or take a dissenter or two

conditional_phrases.only_if: exactly one respondent falls outside the largest bucket (R - largest == 1)

tiers.example: Nearly every nation agrees; one delegation has asked that its dissent be minuted.

phrases: the great majority of city halls
tiers.example: Most nations would show you the water first.

phrases: more capitals than name anything else
tiers.example: A good many countries name the same street.

tie_case._comment: Reached only via step 4, and only when the largest bucket is not unique. It exists because the plurality register can otherwise overclaim at exactly S = 0.5: with 4 respondents split 2-2 there is no bloc that leads, so no plurality phrase is true of it.
tie_case.when: S >= 0.4 and two or more buckets tie for the largest bucket (4 respondents split 2-2, 6 split 3-3, and so on). Exactly two buckets can ever be tied here -- three buckets at 0.4 or more would need a share above 1 -- though smaller buckets may sit underneath them, as in a 2-2-1 split.
phrases: two camps of exactly equal size
level pegging, and the levelness is the story
a tie that neither side will concede

conditional_phrases.phrase: the world is split down the middle
conditional_phrases.only_if: the two tied buckets account for every respondent (2 * largest == R)

tie_case.example: Four city halls answered and split two-two: half the world takes the bus, half the world walks, and neither half will concede a metre.

fragmented_case.when: S < 0.4 -- no bucket reaches the plurality floor -- with R >= min_respondents_for_aggregate. The 3+ threshold is deliberate: a 3-respondent three-way split (1/1/1, S = 0.33) belongs here, not in a 'some countries' register, because there is no agreeing sub-group to point at.
phrases: the community of cities has failed to reach consensus
as many answers as there are answerers, very nearly

conditional_phrases.only_if: every bucket has exactly one member (largest == 1)

fragmented_case.example: On the matter of coriander, the world is divided, and the world would like that on the record.

subgroup_phrasing._comment: Not a tier. This is how the paper points at a notable bucket that is NOT the largest -- two or more mayors who agreed with each other but not with the headline. It was previously a 'minority' tier at min_share 0.2, which was wrong twice over: as a tier it handed the headline to a bucket that had already lost, and once fragmented_case owns everything below 0.4 no distribution could select it.
subgroup_phrasing.example: Most nations rise at seven. Some countries, it turns out, do not believe in breakfast.

outlier_phrasing._comment: Not a tier either -- the bucket-of-one sibling of subgroup_phrasing, for the answer that stood entirely alone. It was previously written as a min_share 0.0 tier, which made it unreachable in practice: any distribution low enough to select it is already fragmented.
outlier_phrasing.example: Most nations named the harbour. One lone municipality answered simply: 'the fog.'

integrity_rules: Pick the tier from the arithmetic first, then write the sentence. Never pick the phrase because it sounds better than the count supports -- 'the world' means every single respondent, not most of them.
If fewer than all mayors answered, say so somewhere in the item ('of the nine who replied...'). An aggregate over 4 of 10 mayors reported as 'the world' is a false statement, not a joke.

Fewer than min_respondents_for_aggregate replies means no aggregate framing at all -- use the low_respondent_floor. The joke of speaking for 'the world' only works when there is a world to speak for; over two answers it is simply inaccurate.
A tie is reported as a tie. If two answers are level, no phrase may imply that either one led -- 'more capitals than name anything else' is simply false at 2-2, which is what tie_case is for.

Selecting the right outcome does not license every wording under it. Anything in 'phrases' is true of every distribution that can select that outcome; anything in 'conditional_phrases' must be checked against the actual counts first. Never reach for the sharper-sounding wording without checking its only_if.
subgroup_phrasing and outlier_phrasing are garnishes, never headlines. The headline claim is whatever step 2-5 selected; a bucket that lost never gets to sound like the aggregate.
A lone or minority answer may be quoted via outlier_phrasing or subgroup_phrasing, but only ever attributed to the city or its mayor's office -- never a real name or handle (spec #28).

Aggregate items must not correlate an answer with an export submission in a way that could identify who submitted what. The questions channel and the blind-voting channel never cross-reference each other (spec #18, #21).
Humour points at the aggregate, at the institution, or at the absurdity of the question -- never at a mayor's answer as a personal failing (spec #30).

_questions_note: Each entry's aggregate_examples has three keys -- unanimous / majority / split -- which are illustrative REGISTERS, not tier ids: they show how this particular question reads at the top of the ladder, in the middle, and when fragmented. They are writing models for the newspaper, not an enum the engine selects from -- 'split' covers both tie_case and fragmented_case. The engine selects an outcome via aggregate_phrasing.ladders.default.selection and then writes in the register those examples demonstrate. 'buckets' names the answer dimension to cluster on before measuring share -- it is a clustering hint, not a closed list, since answers are freeform.

questions.text: Mayor, a visitor has four hours and no plan. What do you show them first?
questions.buckets: kind of place: water / high ground / market or food / a building / a person
questions.newspaper_hook: What the world shows you first

aggregate_examples.unanimous: Shown a stranger and four spare hours, the world takes them to water. Every single nation. No exceptions, no discussion.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations lead with food. A determined minority leads with a view, and one leads with a specific bench.
aggregate_examples.split: Given four hours and a visitor, no two nations agree — the itineraries range from a cathedral to a particular fish counter.

questions.text: Before you were mayor, what did you want to be?
questions.buckets: career family: creative / scientific / hands-on / caring / no idea

aggregate_examples.unanimous: Every mayor in the world wanted to make something with their hands. All of them now attend meetings.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations were headed for a creative life before governance intervened.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's mayors were headed everywhere at once — vets, drummers, engineers, and one who says they always intended exactly this.

questions.text: What is on the mayoral desk that has absolutely no business being there?
questions.buckets: object type: sentimental / edible / broken / borrowed / unidentifiable

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world keeps something sentimental within arm's reach of the official stamp. Every desk. We checked.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most city halls report at least one object nobody can explain and nobody will move.
aggregate_examples.split: Desk audits across the world turned up a rock, a mug of pens that do not work, and one item described only as 'my grandmother's problem now mine'.

questions.text: What time does the mayor actually get up? Not the official answer.
questions.buckets: before 6 / 6-7 / 7-8 / after 8 / varies wildly
questions.newspaper_hook: The hour the world opens its eyes

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world rises before seven, unanimously, and resents it equally.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations are up before seven. A small bloc has quietly opted out of mornings.
aggregate_examples.split: The world wakes at every hour there is, which explains a great deal about scheduling.

questions.text: What food would you refuse to import at any price?
questions.buckets: the named food, clustered by type

aggregate_examples.unanimous: On one point the world is united: nobody wants the olives.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations maintain a standing embargo on the same shellfish.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's personal embargoes overlap nowhere, which is arguably the best news in this edition.

questions.text: Something plays every time you walk into a room. What is it?
questions.buckets: genre / era / mood: triumphal / funny / ominous / sincere

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world enters to brass. Every last delegation. The effect, played simultaneously, would be considerable.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations chose something triumphal; a minority chose something openly threatening.
aggregate_examples.split: No two city halls picked the same entrance music, and one picked silence, 'for effect'.

questions.text: Mayor, what are you genuinely good at that has never once helped you in office?
questions.buckets: physical / musical / craft / memory-trick / social

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world can all do something with its hands that governance has never once required.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations report a musical skill lying entirely fallow.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's unused talents include juggling, whistling through a leaf, and identifying any cheese by smell.

questions.text: When something goes wrong, are you a phone-call mayor or a walk-over-there-yourself mayor?
questions.buckets: phone / walk / 'depends' (counts as its own bucket)
questions.newspaper_hook: How the world responds to bad news

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world walks over there. Not one mayor picks up the phone first.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations go in person. The telephone bloc is small but unrepentant.
aggregate_examples.split: The world is split down the middle on whether to call or to walk, and both halves think the other is being ridiculous.

questions.text: What was the last thing that made you laugh out loud, on your own?
questions.buckets: source: a person / an animal / something online / a mistake / a memory
questions.newspaper_hook: What the world laughed at this week

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world last laughed at an animal doing something ill-advised. Every nation. Independently.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations were last undone by a child or a pet.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's last laughs share no common cause whatsoever, though two involved a bird.

questions.text: Who taught you how to do this job — not the person who was supposed to?
questions.buckets: relation: family / former boss / colleague / stranger / no one

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world learned the job from family. Not one nation credits an institution.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations name someone who was never paid to teach them anything.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's teachers include a grandmother, a night porter, a rival, and, in one case, 'the previous occupant, by counter-example'.

questions.text: The mayoral position on coriander, please. For the record.
questions.buckets: yes / no / genetically doomed / no strong feeling

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world is pro-coriander. This paper considers the matter closed and expects letters.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations are pro-coriander. The opposition is small, loud, and citing genetics.
aggregate_examples.split: On coriander the world is divided, and the world would like that on the record.

questions.text: Where does the mayor go when the mayor wants to be left entirely alone?
questions.buckets: outdoors / vehicle / a room at home / somewhere in the city / nowhere

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world hides outdoors. Every mayor. Not one of them hides in an office.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations retreat to water or high ground; a persistent minority sits in a parked car.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's hiding places range from a stairwell to a specific tree to 'the long way home'.

questions.text: What is the smallest thing that has ever ruined your entire day?
questions.buckets: object failure / social slight / sensory / logistical / self-inflicted

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world can be undone by a small object failing at the wrong moment. Universally.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations name something that broke, spilled, or refused to open.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's small catastrophes include a jammed zip, a misread tone of voice, and one traffic light.

questions.text: Your city is burying a time capsule. What do you put in it personally?
questions.buckets: personal object / document / food / recording / something civic

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world is burying something handwritten. Every nation, without conferring.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations put in a personal object rather than an official one, which tells you something.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's capsules will contain a bus ticket, a recipe, a photograph, and one sealed envelope its mayor declined to describe.

questions.text: What rule do you break constantly and feel completely fine about?
questions.buckets: traffic / food-and-drink / workplace / social convention / their own rule

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world jaywalks. All of it. The world's mayors would like this treated as a technicality.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations admit to a routine traffic offence of some kind.
aggregate_examples.split: The world breaks a different rule each — one of them is a rule that mayor personally introduced.

questions.text: Do you want bad news all at once, or in instalments?
questions.buckets: all at once / instalments / depends on the news

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world wants it all at once. Every nation. Immediately, and preferably standing up.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations want the whole thing at once; a merciful few prefer it in parts.
aggregate_examples.split: The world cannot agree on how it wants to be told, which explains several rounds of this game.

questions.text: Describe one room of the house you lived in at twelve.
questions.buckets: room type + dominant detail (smell / noise / clutter / view / a person in it)

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world remembers a kitchen. Every single one of them. Nobody described a bedroom.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations went straight to the kitchen, and most of those mentioned a radio.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's twelve-year-old rooms have nothing in common but the level of detail, which was considerable.

questions.text: What are you weirdly good at that has no market value at all?
questions.buckets: estimation / recall / physical trick / social read / obscure knowledge

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world can all guess a weight or a distance by eye. This paper finds that faintly unnerving.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations report a talent for remembering something nobody needs remembered.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's unmonetisable talents are entirely distinct, and at least three of them should be televised.

questions.text: If you weren't running a city, what would you be running?
questions.buckets: hospitality / vehicle or vessel / creative outfit / small shop / nothing at all

aggregate_examples.unanimous: Given the choice, the world would be running a small place that serves food. Unanimously. Somebody should look into this.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations would take a bar, a bakery, or a boat.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's alternative commands include a ferry, a bookshop, a stable, and 'absolutely nothing, ever again'.

questions.text: Best thing you have ever eaten standing up?
questions.buckets: street food / market / festival / late night / at home over the sink

aggregate_examples.unanimous: Every nation's finest standing meal was bought on a street from someone who has been making that one thing for years.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations name street food; a candid minority names the kitchen sink at midnight.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's best standing meals have no overlap, though three of them were eaten after 1am.

questions.text: One book, film or album becomes mandatory for the entire council. Which?
questions.buckets: medium: book / film / album; and intent: instructive / pleasurable / punitive

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world would make its councils read. Not one nation chose a film.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations went instructive. A minority chose something purely to see what would happen.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's compulsory syllabus is gloriously incoherent and would take a council eleven weeks to complete.

questions.text: Your honest relationship with mornings, in one sentence.
questions.buckets: loves / tolerates / at war with / has surrendered to

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world is at war with mornings and losing. Every nation reports the same front line.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations describe an uneasy truce with the early hours.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's mornings range from 'the best part of the day' to a single word this paper has chosen not to print.

questions.text: Name a thing everybody else loves that you have never understood.
questions.buckets: food / entertainment / activity / social ritual / technology

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world has never understood the same thing, and it is brunch.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations named a social ritual they attend anyway.
aggregate_examples.split: The world fails to understand a different thing each, and one delegation named this game.

questions.text: Good news arrives. Who do you call first?
questions.buckets: partner / parent / sibling or child / friend / nobody, sits with it

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world calls family first. Every nation. The switchboard confirms.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations call a partner or a parent; a few sit with the news for a while first.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's first calls go in every direction, including one mayor who calls no one and simply goes for a walk.

questions.text: Longest you have ever gone without sleep — and what were you doing?
questions.buckets: cause: work / travel / care / celebration / crisis

aggregate_examples.unanimous: Every nation's longest night was spent looking after somebody else. Every single one.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations were working; a smaller number were celebrating and regret nothing.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's sleepless records range from 20 hours to 'I'd rather not say, legally', with no common cause.

questions.text: A meeting is cancelled and you have a free hour. What actually happens?
questions.buckets: more work / outdoors / food / sleep / something guiltily unproductive
questions.newspaper_hook: What the world does with a free hour

aggregate_examples.unanimous: Given a free hour, the world does more work. This paper finds that a bit grim, frankly.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations go outside. A stubborn bloc simply schedules something else.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's free hour goes to sleep, snacks, errands, and in one case 'a very long shower'.

questions.text: What smell means home?
questions.buckets: cooking / weather or place / plant / industrial or civic / a product

aggregate_examples.unanimous: Home smells of cooking. Everywhere. In every nation on record.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations named something from a kitchen; the rest named weather.
aggregate_examples.split: The world smells of rain on stone, frying onions, diesel, and pine — depending entirely on where you are standing.

questions.text: Your unpopular opinion — the one you would actually defend in public.
questions.buckets: food / culture / technology / etiquette / civic life

aggregate_examples.unanimous: Astonishingly, the world's unpopular opinions were the same opinion, which rather undermines the premise.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations' unpopular opinions concern food, and most of those concern one specific food.
aggregate_examples.split: The world holds eight incompatible unpopular opinions and each mayor is prepared to defend theirs at length.

questions.text: Both options are genuinely fine. How do you decide?
questions.buckets: gut / coin or chance / ask someone / whichever is faster / delay until forced
questions.newspaper_hook: How the world breaks a tie

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world goes with its gut. Every nation. No coins were involved anywhere.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations decide by instinct; a pragmatic minority takes whichever is quicker.
aggregate_examples.split: The world breaks ties by coin, by consultation, by speed, and by waiting until the choice expires.

questions.text: The least practical thing you refuse to throw away?
questions.buckets: paper / clothing / broken tech / ticket or token / inherited object

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world is keeping paper it will never read again. All of it. In a drawer.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations are hoarding something with a date printed on it.
aggregate_examples.split: The world refuses to discard a jacket, a cable, a ticket stub, and one box nobody has opened since the move.

questions.text: First money you ever earned — what did it go on?
questions.buckets: music/media / clothes / food / gift for someone / saved it

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world spent its first wage on music. Every nation. Nobody saved a thing.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations spent it immediately; one or two claim to have saved it and are being believed provisionally.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's first wages went on a bicycle, a jacket, a concert, and one gift for somebody else.

questions.text: If your city vanished overnight, where would you go?
questions.buckets: nearby / same country / abroad / rural / would rebuild in place

aggregate_examples.unanimous: Every nation would rebuild in place. Nobody is leaving. The paper finds this quietly moving.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations would stay close to home; a restless minority named somewhere on another continent.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's contingency plans are scattered across four continents and one mayor's uncle's farm.

questions.text: What are you currently bad at and doing anyway?
questions.buckets: language / instrument / sport / craft / a relationship or habit

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world is learning a language badly. Every nation, simultaneously, and none of them are enjoying it.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations are mid-way through something they are visibly not good at yet.
aggregate_examples.split: The world is currently bad at swimming, Portuguese, chess, and 'saying no', respectively.

questions.text: Describe your ideal Tuesday evening. Be specific.
questions.buckets: alone / with one person / with a group / out / horizontal

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world's ideal Tuesday involves exactly one other person and no plans. Unanimously.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations want to be home by eight. The rest want to be somewhere loud.
aggregate_examples.split: The world's ideal Tuesdays span a football pitch, a bath, a long dinner, and one described only as 'nobody knowing where I am'.

questions.text: What compliment do you actually want to receive?
questions.buckets: competence / kindness / taste / humour / reliability
questions.newspaper_hook: What the world wants said about it

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world wants to be told it is reliable. Every nation chose the least glamorous virtue available.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations want to be found funny, which explains the tone of recent correspondence.
aggregate_examples.split: The world wants to be called clever, kind, funny, and 'sound' — one each, roughly.

questions.text: What is the one thing you would never delegate?
questions.buckets: a specific task / a relationship / a decision type / a domestic thing / nothing
questions.newspaper_hook: What the world keeps for itself

aggregate_examples.unanimous: The world will not delegate an apology. Not one nation would hand that to anybody else.
aggregate_examples.majority: Most nations keep the difficult conversations for themselves.
aggregate_examples.split: The world refuses to delegate a wildly assorted list, including the shopping, the hiring, and one specific hedge.
